entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9990"/><div sID="gen17782" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9990"/><hi type="bold">3. wheels--</hi>literally, "on both stones." The potter's horizontal lathe consisted of two round plates, the lower one larger, the upper smaller; of stone originally, but afterwards of wood. On the upper the potter moulded the clay into what shapes he pleased. They are found represented in Egyptian remains. In <reference osisRef="Exod.1.16">Ex 1:16</reference> alone is the Hebrew word found elsewhere, but in a different sense. <div eID="gen17782" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9992"/><div sID="gen17784" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9992"/>6. Refuting the Jews' reliance on their external privileges as God's elect people, as if God could never cast them off. But if the potter, a mere creature, has power to throw away a marred vessel and raise up other clay from the ground, a fortiori God, the Creator, can cast away the people who prove unfaithful to His election and can raise others in their stead (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.45.9">Is 45:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.64.8">64:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.9.20">Ro 9:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.9.21">21</reference>). It is curious that the potter's field should have been the purchase made with the price of Judas' treachery (<reference osisRef="Matt.27.9">Mt 27:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.27.10">10</reference>: a potter's vessel dashed to pieces, compare <reference osisRef="Ps.2.8">Psa 2:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.9">9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.2.27">Re 2:27</reference>), because of its failing to answer the maker's design, being the very image to depict God's sovereign power to give reprobates to destruction, not by caprice, but in the exercise of His righteous judgment. Matthew quotes Zechariah's words (<reference osisRef="Zech.11.12">Zec 11:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Zech.11.13">13</reference>) as Jeremiah's because the latter (<reference osisRef="Jer.18.1-Jer.19.15">Jr 18:1-19:15</reference>) was the source from which the former derived his summary in <reference osisRef="Zech.11.12">Zec 11:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Zech.11.13">13</reference> [Hengstenberg]. <div eID="gen17784" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 6. Refuting the Jews' reliance on their external privileges as God's elect people, as if God could never cast them off. It is curious that the potter's field should have been the purchase made with the price of Judas' treachery ( Mt 27:9 , 10 : a potter's vessel dashed to pieces, compare Psa 2:8 , 9 ; Re 2:27 ), because of its failing to answer the maker's design, being the very image to depict God's sovereign power to give reprobates to destruction, not by caprice, but in the exercise of His righteous judgment. Matthew quotes Zechariah's words ( Zec 11:12 , 13 ) as Jeremiah's because the latter ( Jr 18:1-19:15 ) was the source from which the former derived his summary in Zec 11:12 , 13 [Hengstenberg].

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9994"/><div sID="gen17786" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9994"/><hi type="bold">8. their evil--</hi>in antithesis to, "the evil that I thought to do."<div eID="gen17786" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17787" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">repent--</hi>God herein adapts Himself to human conceptions. The change is not in God, but in the circumstances which regulate God's dealings: just as we say the land recedes from us when we sail forth, whereas it is we who recede from the land (<reference osisRef="Ezek.18.21">Eze 18:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.33.11">33:11</reference>). God's unchangeable principle is to do the best that can be done under all circumstances; if then He did not take into account the moral change in His people (their prayers, &c.), He would not be acting according to His own unchanging principle (<reference osisRef="Jer.18.9">Jr 18:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.18.10">10</reference>). This is applied practically to the Jews' case (<reference osisRef="Jer.18.11">Jr 18:11</reference>; see <reference osisRef="Jer.26.3">Jr 26:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jonah.3.10">Jon 3:10</reference>). <div eID="gen17787" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9996"/><div sID="gen17790" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9996"/><hi type="bold">12. no hope--</hi>Thy threats and exhortations are all thrown away (<reference osisRef="Jer.2.25">Jr 2:25</reference>). Our case is desperate; we are hopelessly abandoned to our sins and their penalty. In this and the following clauses, "We will walk after our own devices," Jeremiah makes them express the real state of the case, rather than the hypocritical subterfuges which they would have been inclined to put forth. So <reference osisRef="Isa.30.10">Is 30:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.30.11">11</reference>. <div eID="gen17790" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9998"/><div sID="gen17794" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9998"/>14. Is there any man (living near it) who would leave the snow of Lebanon (that is, the cool melted snow water of Lebanon, as he presently explains), which cometh from the rock of the field (a poetical name for Lebanon, which towers aloft above the surrounding field, or comparatively plain country)? None. Yet Israel forsakes Jehovah, the living fountain close at hand, for foreign broken cisterns. <reference osisRef="Jer.17.13">Jr 17:13</reference>; 2:13, accord with English Version here. Maurer translates, "Shall the snow of Lebanon cease from the rock to water (literally, 'forsake') My fields" (the whole land around being peculiarly Jehovah's)? Lebanon means the "white mountain"; so called from the perpetual snow which covers that part called Hermon, stretching northeast of Palestine.<div eID="gen17794" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17795" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that come from another place--</hi>that come from far, namely, from the distant lofty rocks of Lebanon. Henderson translates, "the compressed waters," namely, contracted within a narrow channel while descending through the gorges of the rocks; "flowing" may in this view be rather "flowing down" (<reference osisRef="Song.4.15">So 4:15</reference>). But the parallelism in English Version is better, "which cometh from the rock," "that cometh from another place."<div eID="gen17795" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17796" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">be forsaken--</hi>answering to the parallel, "Will a man leave," &c. Maurer translates, "dry up," or "fail" (<reference osisRef="Isa.19.5">Is 19:5</reference>); the sense thus being, Will nature ever turn aside from its fixed course? The "cold waters" (compare <reference osisRef="Prov.25.25">Pr 25:25</reference>) refer to the perennial streams, fed from the partial melting of the snow in the hot weather. <div eID="gen17796" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10000"/><div sID="gen17803" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10000"/><hi type="bold">16. hissing--</hi>(<reference osisRef="1Kgs.9.8">1Ki 9:8</reference>). In sign of contempt. That which was to be only the event is ascribed to the purpose of the people, although altogether different from what they would have been likely to hope for. Their purpose is represented as being the destruction of their country, because it was the inevitable result of their course of acting.<div eID="gen17803" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17804" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wag ... head--</hi>in mockery (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.21">2Ki 19:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.27.39">Mt 27:39</reference>). entries.reader_content_plain: 17. as with an east wind-- literally, "I will scatter them, as an east wind (scatters all before it)": a most violent wind ( Job 27:21 ; Psa 48:7 ; Is 27:8 ). Thirty-two manuscripts read (without as), "with an east wind." I will show them the back ... not ... face-- just retribution: as "they turned their back unto Me ... not their face" ( Jr 2:27 ).

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10002"/><div sID="gen17807" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10002"/>18. (<reference osisRef="Jer.11.19">Jr 11:19</reference>). Let us bring a capital charge against him, as a false prophet; "for (whereas he foretells that this land shall be left without priests to teach the law, Mal 2:7; without scribes to explain its difficulties; and without prophets to reveal God's will), the law shall not perish from the prophet," &c.; since God has made these a lasting institution in His church, and the law declares they shall never perish (<reference osisRef="Lev.6.18">Le 6:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.10.11">10:11</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Jer.5.12">Jr 5:12</reference>) [Grotius].<div eID="gen17807" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17808" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the wise--</hi>scribes and elders joined to the priests. Perhaps they mean to say, we must have right on our side, in spite of Jeremiah's words against us and our prophets (<reference osisRef="Jer.28.15">Jr 28:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.28.16">16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.29.25">29:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.29.32">32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.5.31">5:31</reference>); "for the law shall not perish," &c. I prefer Grotius' explanation.<div eID="gen17808" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17809" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with ... tongue--</hi>by a false accusation (<reference osisRef="Ps.57.4">Psa 57:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.64.3">64:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.12.4">12:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.50.19">50:19</reference>). "For the tongue" (Margin), that is, for his speaking against us. "In the tongue," that is, let us kill him, that he may speak no more against us [Castalio]. <div eID="gen17809" type="x-p"/>

In the particulars here specified, Jeremiah was a type of Jesus Christ (<reference osisRef="Ps.109.4">Psa 109:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.109.5">5</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.15.25">Joh 15:25</reference>).<div eID="gen17811" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17812" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">my soul--</hi>my life; me (<reference osisRef="Ps.35.7">Psa 35:7</reference>).<div eID="gen17812" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17813" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I stood before thee ... to turn away thy wrath--</hi>so Moses (<reference osisRef="Ps.106.23">Psa 106:23</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.22.30">Eze 22:30</reference>). So Jesus Christ, the antitype of previous partial intercessors (<reference osisRef="Isa.59.16">Is 59:16</reference>). <div eID="gen17813" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10005"/><div sID="gen17814" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10005"/><hi type="bold">21. pour out their blood by the force of the sword--</hi>literally, "by the hands of the sword." So <reference osisRef="Ezek.35.5">Eze 35:5</reference>. Maurer with Jerome translates, "deliver them over to the power of the sword." But compare <reference osisRef="Ps.63.10">Psa 63:10</reference>, Margin; <reference osisRef="Isa.53.12">Is 53:12</reference>. In this prayer he does not indulge in personal revenge, as if it were his own cause that was at stake; but he speaks under the dictation of the Spirit, ceasing to intercede, and speaking prophetically, knowing they were doomed to destruction as reprobates; for those not so, he doubtless ceased not to intercede. We are not to draw an example from this, which is a special case.<div eID="gen17814" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17815" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">put to death--</hi>or, as in <reference osisRef="Jer.15.2">Jr 15:2</reference>, "perish by the death plague" [Maurer].<div eID="gen17815" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17816" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">men ... young men--</hi>Horsley distinguishes the former as married men past middle age; the latter, the flower of unmarried youth. <div eID="gen17816" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10007"/><div sID="gen17819" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10007"/><hi type="bold">23. forgive not--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.109.9">Psa 109:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.10.14">10, 14</reference>).<div eID="gen17819" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17820" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">blot out--</hi>image from an account-book (<reference osisRef="Rev.20.12">Re 20:12</reference>).<div eID="gen17820" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17821" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">before thee--</hi>Hypocrites suppose God is not near, so long as they escape punishment; but when He punishes, they are said to stand before Him, because they can no longer flatter themselves they can escape His eye (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.90.8">Psa 90:8</reference>).<div eID="gen17821" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17822" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">deal thus--</hi>exert Thy power against them [Maurer].<div eID="gen17822" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17823" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">time of thine anger--</hi>Though He seems to tarry, His time shall come at last (<reference osisRef="Eccl.8.11">Ec 8:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.12">12</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.9">2Pe 3:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.10">10</reference>). <chapter eID="Jer.18"/>
entries.content_plain: 23. forgive not-- ( Psa 109:9 , 10, 14 ). blot out-- image from an account-book ( Re 20:12 ). before thee-- Hypocrites suppose God is not near, so long as they escape punishment; but when He punishes, they are said to stand before Him, because they can no longer flatter themselves they can escape His eye (compare Psa 90:8 ). deal thus-- exert Thy power against them [Maurer]. time of thine anger-- Though He seems to tarry, His time shall come at last ( Ec 8:11 , 12 ; 2Pe 3:9 , 10 ).
